categories: ["ก้อน บวม และฝี"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, swollen lymph nodes in the groin are most often a sign that your body is fighting an infection. They can be triggered by a cut on your leg, a urinary tract infection, a sexually transmitted disease, or even a systemic illness. Your doctor will typically examine the lump, ask about other symptoms, and may order blood tests or imaging to identify the underlying cause. Treatment then targets that cause, often with antibiotics or other medications.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment depends entirely on the root cause. For bacterial infections, a course of antibiotics is standard. Over-the-counter pain relievers can help with discomfort, and warm compresses may encourage drainage if an abscess is forming. If the lump persists or looks suspicious, further investigation like an ultrasound or biopsy might be recommended to rule out more serious conditions.
tcm_understanding:
TCM sees groin lumps as a local alarm bell for a deeper internal imbalance. The groin is a crossroads: the Liver channel runs directly through it, and the lower burner is where dampness and heat naturally sink. When your body’s Qi is disrupted - by diet, emotions, or external pathogens - these nodes can swell. That’s why the same lump can have very different origins.
The most common culprit is Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner. Think of it like a steamy, stagnant swamp in your pelvis. Dampness makes the lump feel heavy, wet, and achy; heat makes it red, tender, and possibly oozing. This pattern often comes from eating too many greasy, spicy foods or living in a humid environment.
If that heat intensifies, it can transform into Toxic-Heat - a more aggressive fire that causes the node to become intensely red, throbbing, and filled with pus. You might also feel feverish and thirsty. This is the body’s equivalent of a local fire that needs to be put out fast.
A less common but important pattern is Liver Fire Blazing. The Liver is easily upset by stress, anger, and frustration. When its fire flares, it travels along the channel to the groin, causing swelling that often worsens with emotional upset. You might notice a bitter taste in your mouth and a throbbing headache alongside the lump.
classical_quote: 「横痃者，由风湿毒气客于腠理，与血气相搏，结聚所生也。」
classical_translation: "Inguinal nodules are produced when wind-dampness and toxic qi lodge in the interstices of the skin and flesh, contending with the blood and qi, and binding together to form a mass."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Origins and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Chapter on Inguinal Swelling (横痃候) 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by looking at the nodule itself - its colour, temperature, swelling, and whether there is any discharge. The groin area is traversed by the Liver channel, so the quality of the swelling and the accompanying body-wide signs quickly narrow down which pattern is at play.
If the nodule feels heavy, moist, and swollen with a dull ache, and is accompanied by a greasy yellow tongue coating and a slippery, rapid pulse, Damp-Heat in the Lower Burner is the most likely picture. You might also notice a feeling of heaviness in the legs, cloudy urine, or a thick vaginal discharge. This pattern reflects an accumulation of dampness and heat that has sunk downward.
When the nodule becomes intensely red, hot, and throbbing, and begins to form pus, the pattern has shifted toward Toxic-Heat. Here the tongue is redder, with a dry yellow coating, and the pulse feels rapid and forceful. Systemic signs like fever, thirst, and constipation often appear, signaling that the local inflammation has intensified into a deeper toxicity.
Liver Fire Blazing is less common but can drive swelling along the groin, especially when emotional stress, irritability, or a bitter taste in the mouth are prominent. The nodule may be tender and the skin slightly red, but the key clues are a wiry, rapid pulse and a tongue with red edges. Flank discomfort and headaches often accompany this pattern, reflecting heat rising along the Liver channel.

patterns.symptoms: ["Swollen, tender lymph nodes in the groin", "Foul-smelling vaginal or penile discharge", "Heavy sensation in the lower body", "Burning or painful urination", "Yellow greasy tongue coating thickest at the root", "Slippery, rapid pulse"]
patterns.worse_with: Hot, humid weather, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Prolonged sitting, Stress, anger, or frustration
patterns.better_with: Cool, dry weather, Avoiding greasy and spicy foods, Wearing loose, breathable clothing, Cool compresses, Drinking barley water
patterns.why_this_happens: When dampness and heat accumulate in the lower body, they can obstruct the channels in the groin area. This stagnation causes the lymph nodes to swell, becoming tender, red, and sometimes discharging foul-smelling pus. The heavy, dragging sensation comes from dampness, while heat makes the area feel hot and inflamed.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a thick, yellow greasy coating concentrated at the root. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), often more pronounced at the Chi position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness and heat thrive in hot, humid conditions and are fueled by rich, spicy foods and alcohol. These factors cause the body to produce more damp-heat, which then pours downward to the groin, aggravating the nodules. Cooling, drying measures like loose clothing, cool compresses, and barley water help drain dampness and clear heat, allowing the lymph nodes to recover. Gentle movement also prevents stagnation, which is key in damp-heat patterns.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, spicy, and sweet foods that create dampness and heat. Eat more cooling, drying foods like barley, mung beans, and bitter greens. Keep the groin area clean and dry, wear loose cotton underwear, and avoid sitting for long periods to allow air circulation. Gentle exercise like walking helps Qi flow and reduces dampness.

patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Alcohol, Stress, anger, or frustration, Hot, humid weather, Tight, non-breathable clothing

patterns.why_this_happens: When external pathogenic heat invades deeply or internal fire becomes extreme, it can transform into a noxious toxin. This toxic heat travels through the body and can settle in the groin, where it causes the lymph nodes to become intensely red, swollen, hot, and painful. As the heat toxin intensifies, it can lead to the formation of pus and an abscess that may eventually rupture.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Red body with prickly thorns, dry yellow coating. Pulse: Rapid (shu) and forceful (you li), often full (shi) or overflowing (hong).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic heat is an extreme form of internal heat that thrives on anything that adds more fire - spicy food, alcohol, and emotional stress all fan the flames. Cooling compresses and light foods help drain that excess heat, while rest allows the body's Qi to focus on clearing the toxin. Tight clothing traps heat and moisture in the groin, creating a perfect environment for the toxin to worsen, so loose, breathable fabrics are essential.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat. Eat plenty of cooling, water-rich foods like mung beans, cucumber, watermelon, and leafy greens. Keep the groin area clean and dry, and wear loose, breathable clothing to avoid trapping heat and moisture.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver channel runs through the groin area. When emotional stress or anger causes Liver Fire to blaze, the heat travels along this channel, inflaming the lymph nodes and causing painful, swollen nodules. The fire also rises to the head, producing the classic bitter taste, red eyes, and throbbing headache.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with redder sides, dry yellow coating, possible red prickles. Pulse: wiry and rapid, full and forceful, especially in the left guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and emotional stress directly fuel Liver Fire, causing it to blaze upward and outward along the channel. Alcohol and spicy foods are heating in nature, adding fuel to the fire. Cooling foods and rest help clear heat and calm the Liver, while stress management prevents the emotional sparks that ignite the fire.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, and chrysanthemum tea help clear heat. Avoid alcohol, spicy, and fried foods. Practice stress-reducing activities like meditation or gentle exercise to prevent anger from flaring the fire.

faqs.question: What causes groin lumps in TCM?
faqs.answer: In TCM, groin lumps are caused by an internal buildup of dampness, heat, or toxicity that gets stuck in the groin area. The most common triggers are a diet heavy in greasy, spicy, or sweet foods, a humid living environment, emotional stress, or an external infection that overwhelms the body’s defenses. The exact cause determines which pattern you have - Damp-Heat, Toxic-Heat, or Liver Fire - and guides the treatment.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help swollen lymph nodes in the groin?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can help reduce swelling, pain, and inflammation. Points along the Liver, Spleen, and Stomach channels are used to drain dampness and clear heat from the local area while also calming the whole body. Many patients feel relief after just a few sessions, especially when combined with herbal medicine.

faqs.question: How long until I see results?
faqs.answer: For acute, hot, and painful lumps, you may notice a decrease in pain and redness within the first week of treatment. Swelling usually starts to go down during the second week. If your condition is chronic or keeps coming back, it can take a few months to fully rebalance your body and prevent future episodes.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with antibiotics?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM herbs can safely complement antibiotics. They work in a different way - not by killing bacteria directly but by cooling heat, drying dampness, and supporting your immune system. Always tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor about everything you’re taking. Never stop prescribed antibiotics without your doctor’s approval.

faqs.question: Are there foods I should avoid?
faqs.answer: Yes. Spicy, fried, and greasy foods create more heat and dampness in the body, which can worsen groin lumps. Alcohol, coffee, and excessive sugar have the same effect. Focus on cooling, lightly cooked foods like cucumber, mung beans, and leafy greens, and drink plenty of water to help flush out toxins.

faqs.question: Will the lumps come back after treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to prevent recurrence by fixing the underlying imbalance. If you complete the full course of treatment and make the recommended diet and lifestyle changes, the likelihood of the lumps returning drops significantly. For chronic conditions, occasional tune-up treatments can help maintain balance.
